prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form, which established the physiological basis for GLP-1-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: B017 alone, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case does not depend on the six-way agreement. It is an unbroken chain from gut-hormone physiology (secretion and action of GLP-1 in humans, proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) form) to a drug class with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It is original, independently confirmed over decades, and mature. A citation anchored on the hormone and its active form keeps the award within physiology or medicine and states the omission of the long-acting analogue step as a principle, not an oversight. I now weigh the central appetite effects less than in round 1, as the peripheral incretin physiology and the outcome data carry the case. I see no second part that is as complete as B017, so I do not add one.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point and I do not think the wording fully removes it. The Mojsov priority question for the active peptide cannot be settled from the supplied record, Habener and other early investigators are outside the supplied names, and leaving out Knudsen means the committee honours the discovery but not the design of liraglutide and semaglutide, which changed practice. If members who weigh that omission heavily are right, the award would look incomplete. A second part (B006 or B024) would add scientific weight but also a new attribution problem (Eshhar for B006, Rowley and upstream BCR-ABL work for B024), and it would dilute a first part that is much cleaner scientifically.

responses.point: Calls the Mojsov versus Knudsen choice a close call, having moved from an opening ballot that included Knudsen, and notes that a physiology prize without drug design can look incomplete.
responses.response: I agree it is close and I do not claim my choice is clearly superior. I still keep Mojsov because identification of the active peptide is a discovery that the later pharmacology depends on, whereas Knudsen's contribution is optimisation of a known mechanism. Your suggestion that the citation can acknowledge the analogues without making Knudsen necessary is the point I would test. I would not name the analogues in the citation, because naming them would invite the question of why their designer is absent. I would instead keep the citation on the hormone and its active form.

responses.point: As chair, asks whether the third seat should go to Mojsov or Knudsen and whether the Mojsov versus Habener priority question can be resolved from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: On the chair's second question, I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence and I will not pretend otherwise. What I can say is that no member has produced evidence that favours Habener over Mojsov, and the supplied credit lists Mojsov for the active peptide. If the priority question is unresolved, the safer choice is the citation worded on the hormone and its active form, with the dispute stated in the committee's record. I also keep my view from round 1 that the central appetite effects should not carry the citation, in agreement with your reading.

responses.point: Accepts the credit gap as a cost but says it should be stated openly, and limits B006 to June and Sadelain without Rosenberg.
responses.response: I agree that the gap should be stated openly in the committee record and not treated as settled. For B006, I now follow your narrower version as my alternative, June and Sadelain, because Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a related but separate line. The Eshhar gap remains for me as the main reason I would not add B006 as a second part in this configuration. My alternatives list is therefore a statement of what I would turn to if B017 failed, not a request for a pairing.

responses.point: Treats Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the most defensible set that rewards discovery over product development, and sees B024 mainly as drug development with upstream work outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with your reading of B024 as drug development, and I keep B024 only as a lower alternative. Your point sharpens my view that B006 would be the more defensible second option if the committee wanted one. I would add one qualification to your discovery-versus-development framing. The same line separates a discovery from the drug that applies it in B017 itself, where Knudsen is on the other side of that line. If we apply it to B017 we should apply it consistently to B024, and we do.

responses.point: Moved from a trio with Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and asks whether a second distinct part such as CAR-T or anti-TNF is worth the attribution cost under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I take your cost argument seriously and it is the reason I do not add a second part. A second part is worth it only if its attribution is as defensible as B017, and I do not think B006 or B018 meets that bar from the supplied names. I note your move away from Knudsen as a useful sign that the physiology reading can be held across the committee. I do not use that as a reason to prefer it, since support counts are not a substitute for the scientific case.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a physiology-centred award or one that also covers development of long-acting analogues, which decides whether Mojsov or Knudsen takes the third seat.
Priority for the active GLP-1 peptide among Mojsov, Habener and others, which I have not independently verified.
Whether B006 can be given a defensible attribution without Eshhar, and whether any second part would improve the award more than it complicates the credit.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B017 or the alternatives B006 and B024 is documented in my profile. My ties (Grillner, Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) concern motor circuits and neuron biology, not shortlisted candidates. Optogenetics (B049) touches my field, and I do not propose it. I request no recusal.
